newsitem.title: ITALY: Kinkel delays trip to Turkey after Erbakan remarks.
newsitem.headline: Kinkel delays trip to Turkey after Erbakan remarks.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel set off for Turkey two hours late on Tuesday after delaying his departure from Rome to check controversial comments attributed to Turkey's Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan.
The foreign ministry entourage travelling with Kinkel said he had delayed setting off to inspect media reports quoting Erbakan as saying Kinkel should come to Turkey with his head hung in shame.
A ministry spokesman said Kinkel decided the comments were not meant in the way interpreted and would proceed with his visit.
The Turkish embassy in Bonn said Erbakan's comments had been incorrectly reported by one German news agency.
Ahead of Kinkel's visit, Erbakan said Turkey should be treated with more respect internationally.
Erbakan told a meeting of MPs from his Islamist Welfare Party Turkey had incurred losses because of a customs accord with the EU that went into effect at the start of 1996.
"There will be a $5 billion loss for Turkey because it has entered the customs union... After they have done this they will bow their heads when they talk with Turkey," Erbakan said.
EU exports to Turkey have surged under the accord, while Turkish exports to the bloc have changed little.

"It will be very interesting to meet with him (Kinkel). Now nobody can give Turkey the 'do this, do that' treatment... The respect and treatment which the new world leader Turkey deserves will be realised," he said.
Kinkel was due to arrive in Ankara on Tuesday evening and meet Erbakan and Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller on Wednesday. He goes to Istanbul on Thursday.
During his visit Kinkel is expected to try to appease NATO ally Turkey over the continued EU rejection of Ankara's long-standing bid to join the bloc.

Europe's Christian Democrat leaders, including Germany's Chancellor Helmut Kohl, said earlier this month that Turkey's Moslem culture made it unfit to join the EU. Kinkel and other EU foreign ministers have distanced themselves from these statements.
Millions of dollars in EU transitonal aid have been blocked by Greece over disputes in Cyprus and the Aegean and by EU states concerned about Ankara's human rights record.
Turkey has been an associate member of the EU since 1963 and regards it as unjust that other states, including former east European adversaries, might get into the EU before Ankara.
Some European leaders fear that distancing Turkey from Europe could lead the country, officially secular but with an overwhelmingly Moslem population, to turn towards other Moslem countries instead.
